extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato's Republic; readers interested in ancient moral and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the normative definitions, argumentative criteria, and examples Plato (via Socrates, Thrasymachus, Glaucon) uses to characterize and evaluate 'justice' and related concepts in Book I–II of the Republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is the interest of the stronger (Thrasymachus' definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the interest of the stronger / the ruler: what the superior commands as being to his interest is justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thrasymachus asserts that rulers (in their capacity as rulers) command what is for their interest and that subjects obeying those commands is justice. He initially allows rulers may err, but then insists that, strictly speaking, a ruler as ruler is unerring and thus always commands his own interest. He uses this to claim that injustice (when on a large scale) is more profitable than justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler-as-unerring formulation (strict sense of 'ruler')
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'ruler' is taken in the strict sense, the ruler, in so far as he is a ruler, is unerring and always commands that which is for his own interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thrasymachus distinguishes a 'strict' sense of ruler (the true ruler as an expert) and argues that in that strict sense the ruler cannot be mistaken about what is in his interest; Socrates questions and problematizes this claim by analogy with arts (physician, pilot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts/rulers aim at the good of their subjects (Socratic refutation principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each genuine art or true ruler, in so far as it is what its name implies, attends to the good of its subject (e.g., physician to the body, pilot to sailors, shepherd to sheep) rather than to the good of the superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates uses analogies: the true physician heals the sick for the patient's good; the true pilot rules sailors for their safety; the art's aim is the perfection/well-being of its subject. This undermines Thrasymachus' claim that rulers necessarily legislate for their own interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: The interest of an art is the perfection of its subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The interest/aim of any art is the perfection of its subject-matter (e.g., medicine cares for the body, horsemanship for the horse); arts do not consider their own advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates argues that arts remain 'pure and faultless' while true, and they care only for the subject of their art. Examples: medicine's interest is the health of the body; horsemanship the good of the horse. The argument distinguishes the ends proper to each art from ancillary goods (like pay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment or compulsion needed for good men to govern
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the best men do not seek office for money or honour, they are induced to rule either by remuneration (money or honour) or by compulsion/penalty for refusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates suggests three 'modes of payment' to explain why good people might accept governance: money, honour, or a penalty compelling service; otherwise good men avoid ruling because it is burdensome and not self-rewarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as the excellence/virtue of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is identified as the excellence (virtue) of the soul, whereas injustice is its defect; the just soul is wise/good, the unjust soul ignorant/evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through dialectic, Socrates leads admissions that the just is like wisdom and virtue and the unjust like vice and ignorance. This identification supports further claims about the consequences for life and happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice undermines unity and collective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice creates divisions, hatred, and internal strife; therefore bodies (states, armies, gangs) composed of unjust persons are incapable of unified, effective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates argues that while unjust persons might appear powerful, large-scale injustice produces faction and incapacity for joint action; he uses the example that truly villainous groups would fight among themselves without some remnant of justice to hold them together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological account: things have an end and an excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every thing (organs, tools, beings) has an end/function which it fulfills by its proper excellence; lacking that excellence prevents the fulfillment of its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates illustrates with eyes, ears, pruning-hooks and horses: each has an end that only its proper excellence can achieve. He applies this to the soul: the soul's ends (deliberation, rule, life) require the soul's excellence; thus a 'good' soul fulfills its ends, a bad soul fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: A good (excellent) soul leads to living well and happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: If justice is the excellence of the soul, then the just man (having a good soul) will live well and be happy; the unjust man, with an evil soul, will live ill and be miserable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates deduces that since living well is what makes one blessed/happy and justice is the soul's excellence, justice is profitable insofar as it produces happiness—thereby refuting Thrasymachus' claim that injustice is more profitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of goods (three classes) and the question of where justice belongs
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods are classifiable into: (1) desired for their own sake (harmless pleasures), (2) desired for their results (knowledge, sight, health), and (3) desired both for themselves and results (some gymnastic/medical labors, money-making). The question is which class justice belongs to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glaucon raises this taxonomy to challenge Socrates: many people view justice as a third-class good (pursued for reputation/reward, not for itself), while Socrates places it among the highest goods desired both for itself and for its results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common/popular view: justice practised unwillingly as a social contract
rubrics_metrics.description: The common view (revived by Glaucon) is that people practice justice not because it is intrinsically good but from necessity—they agree to limit actions for mutual advantage; justice is therefore a compromise and not a real good in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glaucon proposes to restate and strengthen Thrasymachus' position by arguing first from the 'common view' of the origin/nature of justice, then that people act justly out of necessity, and finally that the unjust life is better—setting up Socrates' fuller inquiry in Book II.
